newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW - Australian Nov employment data.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW - Australian Nov employment data.

text.p: Australian employment rose 24,400 in November and the unemployment rate fell to 8.5 percent from 8.8 in October, official figures released on Thursday showed.
Economists' median forecasts had centred on a rise of 10,000 in employment levels and an unemployment rate of 8.7 percent.
A selection of economists' immediate reactions to the data follow.
TIM PFITZNER, ECONOMIST, NATIONAL AUSTRALIA BANK:

"It is a little bit stonger than what we were expecting ... My suspicion was that perhaps because the retail sector has been so soft that a lot of the employment around this time of year hadn't been coming through, and that might have kept the number a little bit stronger. Nonetheless, you add it up over the last couple of months, it's still not a pattern of employment growth that's really taking off. We're still watching it pretty cautiously."
STEPHEN HALMARICK, BOND AND CURRENCY STRATEGIST, NATWEST:

"The number of people employed was up a little bit stronger than the market had expected, and the unemployment level down to its lowest level since July. But the bond market had been weakening off quite sharply ahead of the number ... and I'm afraid our traders have basically all but ignored the employment number and it is offshore factors that are really driving the market at the moment."
MICHAEL BLYTHE, SENIOR ECONOMIST, COMMONWEALTH BANK:

"We were expecting a rise of 25,000 so the figure for November when it came in was not a surprise to us. This fall in umemployment as well as the recent rate cuts should be a bit of a confidence booster for retailers over Christmas."
HANS KUNNEN, CHIEF ECONOMIST, COLONIAL STATE BANK:

"The trend unemployment rate is still weak, the unemployment rate hasn't fallen in trend terms, and that still suggests the economy is not firing on all six cylinders. No immediate implications for policy. I think we'll have to wait and see the effects of the rate cuts so jobs growth may be a bit stronger in three or four months' time. This figure maintains the pattern of the last few months where jobs growth has been modest -- that would be the best description."
BRUCE HOCKMAN, SENIOR ECONOMIST, DEUTSCHE MORGAN GRENFELL:

"I think our interpretation of the numbers we are seeing is that still growth looks on track -- nothing impressive or spectacular -- and certainly nothing that makes you think there has been any sort of pressure on prices coming through from the labour market other than is what happening in the enterprise barganining sector already. I shouldn't think the rate cuts are having an impact yet."
JOHN PETERS, ECONOMIST, WESTPAC BANKING CORP:

"While it came in at the top of the market range for employment growth, a lot of that was part-time. If you look at the growth, about 61,000 jobs have been created over the first 11 months of 1996, so it doesn't really alter our view that labour market conditions are pretty weak. The labour market growth is not strong enough to push down the unemployment rate, and looking at the forward indicators we think it will push up in the coming months."
STEPHEN ROBERTS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, UBS AUSTRALIA:

"The figures are reasonably firm. It does appear as if the worst of the softness in the labour market is now in the past. Net result is that the unemployment rate has come back a little to 8.5 percent -- the lowest unemployment reading we've seen over the last four or five months. It's starting to work its way downwards again. It suggests that perhaps the employment market is difficult to rationalise still. It does appear that economic activity is starting to accelerate and the unemployment rate is a lagging indicator. Even this lagging indicator is showing some signs of improvement."
STEPHEN KOUKOULAS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, CITIBANK AUSTRALIA:

"They're pleasantly strong. Maybe the worst in the labour market is being negotiated now. It's a bit early to say that the worst is over, but there's signs that there's a bit of employment growth coming through clearly, a bit of a consolidation of the unemployment rate between this 8.5 and 8.75 percent rather than the feared 9.0 percent being hit. I think there's some pretty good reasons to think that while we still might get a slight drifting up in the unemployment rate in the next few months, that by around the June quarter next year we might be seing some signs of life in the labour market on the back of the expected pick up in the whole economy."
